classification.difficultyReason: Use two scaffolded congruence proofs to establish midpoint and perpendicular consequences without assuming the common-chord theorem.

content.prompt:
Prove that: When two circles intersect, the line joining their centres is the perpendicular bisector of their common chord.
Let two circles with centres O and P intersect at F and G. Let OP meet the common chord FG at M.

spec.description: Two intersecting circles, with larger circle centred at O on the left and smaller circle centred at P on the right. Their intersections are G above and F below. The horizontal segment OP crosses the common chord FG at M. Segments OG, OF, PG and PF are drawn. O and P are red points; circle outlines and segments are blue. Labels O, P, F, G and M are visible. No right-angle marker or equal-length marks are supplied.
spec.answerVisibility: All original givens/point identities retained, no computed student values or added proof segments.

answer.worked: OF=OG (radii of the first circle), PF=PG (radii of the second), and OP is common. Thus $\triangle FOP\equiv\triangle GOP$ (SSS).
Part a gives $\angle FOP=\angle GOP$. Since M lies on OP, $\angle FOM=\angle GOM$. Also OF=OG (radii) and OM is common, so $\triangle FOM\equiv\triangle GOM$ (SAS).

children.label: c
children.prompt: Hence, prove that FM = GM and OP ⟂ FG.

answer.worked: Matching sides in part b give FM=GM. Matching angles FMO and GMO are equal and form a straight angle, so each is $90^\circ$. As O,M,P are collinear, $OP\perp FG$.
